title: Operating Systems Foundations
description: Kernel, syscalls, processes, and isolation — the contract between program and machine, taught the xv6 way: small enough to hold.

sourceReferences.title: MIT 6.1810 Operating System Engineering
sourceReferences.notes: Hardware/software contract first. xv6 as a complete small Unix.

sourceReferences.title: xv6 book
sourceReferences.notes: Organization, traps, isolation before locks and filesystems.

modules.title: The kernel as a program
learningObjectives: Treat the kernel as the program that owns the machine
Name privilege, traps, and syscalls as the crossing

modules.title: Processes
learningObjectives: Treat a process as an isolated address space
Use fork, exec, and wait as the process API

modules.title: Leaving and returning
modules.blurb: Interrupts, context switch, devices at a glance.
learningObjectives: Explain a context switch as saving one life and restoring another
Treat interrupts as devices entering the kernel

concepts.name: The kernel
concepts.summary: The program that owns the machine and rents it out.
objectives: Explain the kernel as the program that owns the machine and rents it to user programs
Name what the kernel mediates that a lone program cannot safely do itself

concepts.name: Privilege rings
concepts.summary: User code that cannot issue the dangerous instructions.
objectives: Distinguish privileged instructions from ordinary user-mode execution
Predict what happens when user code tries a privileged operation

concepts.name: System calls
concepts.summary: The narrow door a process uses to ask for work.
objectives: Describe a system call as the narrow door a program uses to request kernel work
Trace user request, privilege crossing, kernel action, and return

concepts.name: Traps and exceptions
concepts.summary: How control transfers into the kernel without a CALL.
objectives: Explain a trap as a controlled transfer into the kernel that is not an ordinary CALL
Distinguish a requested syscall trap from an unexpected exception

concepts.name: User versus kernel memory
concepts.summary: Two maps, one CPU, a lot of checking.
objectives: Contrast user-accessible memory with memory the kernel keeps for itself
Predict why the kernel must check pointers a program hands it

concepts.name: The syscall ABI
concepts.summary: Registers, numbers, and the compatibility tax.
objectives: Describe the syscall ABI as the register and number contract both sides honour
Predict why changing that contract breaks old binaries

concepts.name: A small Unix as a map
concepts.summary: xv6 as a complete system you can finish reading.
objectives: Treat xv6 as a complete small Unix you can finish reading
Locate kernel, syscalls, and processes on that map without needing later chapters

concepts.name: Booting
concepts.summary: From reset vector to the first process.
objectives: Trace the machine from reset to a kernel that can run a first process
Name what must exist before the first user program can start

concepts.name: Processes and threads
concepts.summary: Address spaces, threads, and what isolation actually costs.
objectives: Describe a process as an address space plus the threads that run in it
Name the isolation a process is supposed to provide, and that it is not free

concepts.name: Threads versus processes
concepts.summary: Shared address space versus a private one.
objectives: Contrast threads that share an address space with processes that do not
Predict what a wild write in one thread can do to its siblings

concepts.name: Isolation
concepts.summary: A crash next door should be someone else's problem.
objectives: Explain isolation as a crash next door remaining someone else's problem
Diagnose a simple isolation failure when two programs share more than they should

concepts.name: fork
concepts.summary: Copy the process, then diverge.
objectives: Describe fork as copying a process so parent and child can then diverge
Predict which state the child starts with and how the two then differ

concepts.name: exec
concepts.summary: Replace the address space, keep the process id.
objectives: Describe exec as replacing the address space while keeping the process identity
Predict what survives exec and what is overwritten

concepts.name: wait
concepts.summary: Reaping children so they do not stay zombies.
objectives: Explain wait as reaping a child so it does not remain a zombie
Predict what happens to a dead child if no parent waits

concepts.name: The shell as a user of the API
concepts.summary: A loop of fork, exec, wait that invents scripting.
objectives: Describe the shell as a user program looping fork, exec, and wait
Predict how that loop becomes a script of commands

concepts.name: Protection domains
concepts.summary: Who may touch which object.
objectives: Describe a protection domain as a rule about who may touch which object
Predict a denial when a process touches an object outside its domain

concepts.name: Kernel structure
concepts.summary: Monoliths, microkernels, and the argument about where the driver lives.
objectives: Contrast a kernel that contains drivers with one that keeps them in user space
Predict what a driver crash costs in each structure

concepts.name: Context switches
concepts.summary: Saving one life and restoring another.
objectives: Describe a context switch as saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's
Predict what must be saved for the first process to resume correctly

concepts.name: Interrupts
concepts.summary: The device rings; the kernel answers.
objectives: Describe an interrupt as a device forcing a transfer into the kernel
Contrast an interrupt with a trap the current program requested

concepts.name: Devices as files of a sort
concepts.summary: A register file on the other side of a bus.
objectives: Describe a device as registers on a bus that the kernel mediates
Explain why programs usually see devices through file-like handles rather than raw registers

concepts.name: IPC, first look
concepts.summary: Pipes and messages before shared-memory races.
objectives: Describe IPC as how processes exchange data without sharing an address space
Contrast a pipe or message with two processes writing the same memory

concepts.name: Batch, multiprogramming, time-share
concepts.summary: Why we started switching at all.
objectives: Contrast batch, multiprogramming, and time-sharing as reasons to switch
Predict why a machine started switching instead of running one job to completion
